articles.title: Net zero emissions won’t reverse climate change — some nations look to ‘net negative’
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03789-3Countries are starting to grapple with the reality that bringing temperatures down after they breach the 1.5 ºC target would require removingmassive amounts of carbon dioxide from the air.
articles.content:
A display reminds those attending the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, of their goal: limiting global warming to 1.5 ºC.Credit: Metin Aktas/Anadolu/Getty

Net zero is no longer enough. Among countries at the COP31 climate summit under way in Antalya, Turkey, there’s a growing recognition that meeting climate targets will require the world to go ‘net negative’, which means removal of more carbon dioxide from the air than is added.

Scientists say that climate ‘overshoot’ — exceeding 1.5 °C of warming, a target set in 2015 in the landmark Paris Agreement — is now inevitable in the next few years. Reaching net-zero status would halt the rise in temperatures. But only achieving net-negative status can bring temperatures back below the 1.5 °C threshold this century.

Can AI actually help the climate? Nations want to harness the technology to cut emissions

That reality has made net negative and the enormous amount of CO 2 removal that would be needed to achieve it a prominent idea at the summit. A coalition of eight countries called the Group of Negative Emitters (GONE) has been working to convince other nations to adopt net-negative targets and get serious about CO 2 removal. The group announced that it will be co-chaired by Denmark and Ethiopia, which is hosting next year’s climate summit and could put net negative at the top of the agenda.

“We are in an era of overshoot, and we have to do a lot in terms of removing carbon dioxide,” Ethiopian ambassador Samuel Addis Alemayehu said at a GONE event on 18 November, touting the nation’s progress on reforestation.

Some climate campaigners worry that CO 2 removal technologies won’t work and that focusing on them could distract countries from cutting emissions. Despite those concerns, the latest draft of the main statement from COP31 recognizes that CO 2 removal has a role in addressing the overshoot, and welcomes efforts to “urgently and rapidly” scale up development of removal methods.

The overshoot COP

According to a United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) report1 released ahead of the meeting, the world can expect about 1.8 °C of warming this century, even in the most optimistic emissions scenario.

Every fraction of a degree above 1.5 °C raises the risk of climate disasters such as wildfires and powerful hurricanes. “COP31 will be judged a failure if we don’t address the overshoot,” said Ilana Seid, Palau’s ambassador to the UN and chair of the Association of Small Island States, at a press briefing held during the summit.

Many countries at the meeting have discussed slashing emissions to limit the size and duration of the coming overshoot. Turkey has pushed to implement a target of 35% of global energy demand being met with electricity by 2035, a proposal that has gained support from more than 75 countries at the conference and is also included in the draft statement.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on a significant and inspiring shift in global climate policy at COP31, where nations acknowledge that net zero emissions alone are insufficient and are moving toward net negative emissions to actively reduce atmospheric CO2 and reverse temperature rise. This represents a meaningful, large-scale environmental commitment with broad impact for global climate action, supported by concrete international cooperation and emerging strategies.

**Context** – The world agreed in 2015 to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius to avoid severe climate problems. Countries have been working to cut emissions to net zero, meaning they add no more carbon dioxide (CO2) to the air than they remove. But scientists now say this may not be enough.

**What happened** – At the COP31 climate summit in Turkey in November 2026, countries recognized that temperatures will likely go above 1.5 °C soon. To lower temperatures again, they must remove more CO2 from the air than they emit, called going 'net negative.' A group called the Group of Negative Emitters (GONE), made up of eight countries, is pushing others to adopt these stronger goals. Denmark and Ethiopia will lead this group next year.

**Impact** – This shift shows that countries are ready to take bigger steps to fight climate change. Instead of just stopping emissions, they want to pull CO2 out of the atmosphere, which could help cool the planet. This is important because even a small rise above 1.5 °C increases risks like wildfires and hurricanes. The summit also saw support for new targets, such as producing 35% of global energy from electricity by 2035.

**What's next step** – Next year’s climate summit in Ethiopia will focus on net-negative goals, pushing countries to develop and use technologies to remove CO2 faster. Meanwhile, countries will work on cutting emissions as much as possible to reduce how high and how long temperatures rise.

**One-sentence takeaway** – At COP31, nations agreed that going beyond net zero to remove more CO2 than they emit is essential to lower global temperatures and reduce climate risks.

articles.title: These gaps in weather data affect forecasts everywhere: plugging them is not charity
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03811-8Investing in observations in low-income countries will help to prevent climate disasters worldwide.
articles.content:
Observations from data-scarce regions, such as low-lying island Tuvalu in the South Pacific, are crucial to weather forecasts, early warning systems and climate-information services elsewhere. Credit: Mario Tama/Getty

When I talk about collecting essential weather and climate data in countries with limited resources, many take it to mean that wealthier countries, institutions and firms should ‘help poorer ones’. But as a development and climate-finance executive, I know that this is an investment rather than an act of charity. Science proves it: better forecasts at home rely on observations abroad.

That’s the resounding conclusion of a report published this month by The European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) in collaboration with the World Meteorological Organization (WMO). The report was commissioned by the Systematic Observations Financing Facility (SOFF), a United Nations fund dedicated to basic weather and climate data around the world, of which I am a director.

Its aim was to establish the benefits of filling gaps in the WMO’s Global Basic Observing Network (GBON), which defines member nations’ mandatory weather-station coverage. To comply, each country must have a land station every 200 kilometres, as well as a weather balloon every 500 kilometres over land and every 1,000 kilometres over sea to collect data on essential variables (such as temperature, pressure, humidity and wind).

Global climate body fights for survival: why the IPCC must be saved

But agreeing on standards and sites is not the same as having the economic means to implement them. Since 2023, GBON stations have been required to share their data. Yet, about 90% of weather data from low-income countries and small island nations are not being shared. Some data are not even collected because many stations are missing, stopped working or cannot transmit their measurements.

These gaps don’t just impede local forecasts, they affect regional and global projections too. Daily weather data feed into increasingly sophisticated computer models that predict how weather systems around the world evolve.

Think of a weather forecast as a photograph. It is made up of millions of pixels, each contributing a small piece of information. Weather forecasting is more complex, but the analogy helps to explain the problem: if too many ‘pixels’ are missing, the global picture is blurry or incomplete. And for forecasts, some ‘pixels’, or observations, are more valuable than others. Plugging gaps in data-scarce regions is the best way to improve forecasts everywhere.

It is also a matter of justice: on average, a seven-day temperature forecast in a high-income country is as accurate as a one-day forecast in a low-income country (M. Linsenmeier and J. G. Shrader Nature Commun. 17, 10792; 2026).

The results of the ECMWF simulations are striking. Better coverage in low-income countries and small island states can cut uncertainty in 12-hour local forecasts by more than 30% in parts of Africa and by up to 20% across the Pacific.

Extra data in all countries eligible for development assistance and small island nations would improve the accuracy of temperature and wind forecasts up to six or seven days ahead in the tropics, home to some 40% of the world’s population, and in the Northern Hemisphere’s mid-latitudes, where much of Europe, North America and northern Asia sit. This would help with, for example, aviation and maritime operations, planning of agricultural activities, water management and preparations for severe weather.

Disparity in countries’ capacity to finance weather observations is striking. To quantify the inequality, SOFF developed an indicator comparing countries’ gross dom-estic product (GDP) with the geographical area for which they are mandated to provide observations, including marine exclusive economic zones. For example, although it is a small country, Switzerland has a larger budget than does Tuvalu, a Pacific island nation spread across an immense ocean area (Switzerland’s GDP is around 300,000 times larger per square kilometre). Yet both countries contribute to and benefit from the same global observing system.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights the critical importance of investing in weather and climate data collection in low-income countries to improve global weather forecasts and early warning systems. This has broad, meaningful benefits for climate disaster prevention worldwide, impacting large populations and multiple sectors such as agriculture, aviation, and water management. The story focuses on a significant global environmental challenge with detailed context and evidence, emphasizing justice and global cooperation.
articles.personality_title: Investing in weather data from poorer countries improves forecasts worldwide
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Weather forecasts rely on data collected from many places around the world. Some countries, especially low-income ones and small island nations, do not have enough weather stations or the means to share their data. This creates gaps in the global information needed for accurate weather predictions.

**What happened** – A new report from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) and the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) shows that filling these gaps by supporting weather stations in poorer countries can greatly improve weather forecasts everywhere. The report highlights that since 2023, countries must share weather data as part of the Global Basic Observing Network (GBON), but about 90% of data from low-income countries is missing or not shared.

**Impact** – Missing weather data from certain regions makes forecasts less accurate not only locally but worldwide. The report’s computer simulations found that better weather data in poorer countries can reduce forecast uncertainty by up to 30% in parts of Africa and 20% in the Pacific. This improvement helps people prepare for storms, manage farming, and plan transportation like flights and ships. It also points out an inequality: rich countries have far more resources to collect data, even if their land area is smaller than some poorer countries.

**What's next step** – The United Nations’ Systematic Observations Financing Facility (SOFF) is working to fund and support weather stations in these data-scarce countries. The goal is to close the gaps in the global observing network so that all countries can share reliable weather information, improving forecasts and safety worldwide.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Supporting weather data collection in poorer countries strengthens global forecasts, making weather predictions more accurate for everyone.
articles.personality_title_fr: Investir dans les données météorologiques des pays pauvres améliore les prévisions mondiales
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les prévisions météorologiques dépendent des données recueillies dans le monde entier. Certains pays, surtout les pays à faible revenu et les petites îles, manquent de stations météo ou ne peuvent pas partager leurs données, ce qui crée des lacunes dans les informations nécessaires.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Un nouveau rapport du Centre européen pour les prévisions météorologiques à moyen terme (ECMWF) et de l’Organisation météorologique mondiale (OMM) montre qu’en comblant ces lacunes grâce au soutien des stations météo dans les pays pauvres, on peut améliorer fortement les prévisions partout. Depuis 2023, les pays doivent partager leurs données selon le Réseau mondial d’observation de base (GBON), mais environ 90 % des données des pays pauvres manquent ou ne sont pas partagées.

**Impact** – L’absence de données météo dans certaines régions rend les prévisions moins précises localement et dans le monde entier. Les simulations du rapport montrent qu’une meilleure collecte dans les pays pauvres peut réduire l’incertitude des prévisions de 30 % en Afrique et de 20 % dans le Pacifique. Cela aide à mieux se préparer aux tempêtes, gérer l’agriculture et organiser les transports comme les avions et les navires. Le rapport souligne aussi une inégalité : les pays riches ont beaucoup plus de ressources pour collecter les données, même si leur territoire est plus petit.

**Prochaine étape** – Le Fonds de financement des observations systématiques (SOFF) des Nations Unies travaille à financer et soutenir les stations météo dans ces pays, pour combler les lacunes du réseau mondial et améliorer la sécurité et les prévisions partout.

**Conclusion en une phrase** – Soutenir la collecte de données météo dans les pays pauvres renforce les prévisions mondiales, rendant les prévisions plus précises pour tous.
articles.personality_title_es: Invertir en datos meteorológicos de países pobres mejora las predicciones globales
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Las predicciones del clima dependen de datos recogidos en todo el mundo. Algunos países, especialmente los de bajos ingresos y las pequeñas islas, no tienen suficientes estaciones meteorológicas ni medios para compartir sus datos, lo que crea vacíos en la información necesaria.

**Qué pasó** – Un nuevo informe del Centro Europeo para Pronósticos Meteorológicos a Medio Plazo (ECMWF) y la Organización Meteorológica Mundial (OMM) muestra que llenar estos vacíos apoyando estaciones meteorológicas en países pobres puede mejorar mucho las predicciones en todo el mundo. Desde 2023, los países deben compartir datos según la Red Global de Observación Básica (GBON), pero alrededor del 90 % de los datos de países pobres no se comparten o no se recogen.

**Impacto** – La falta de datos meteorológicos en ciertas regiones hace que las predicciones sean menos precisas tanto local como globalmente. Las simulaciones del informe indican que mejorar la cobertura en países pobres puede reducir la incertidumbre de las predicciones hasta un 30 % en partes de África y un 20 % en el Pacífico. Esto ayuda a prepararse para tormentas, manejar la agricultura y planificar transporte como vuelos y barcos. También destaca una desigualdad: los países ricos tienen muchos más recursos para recolectar datos, aunque su territorio sea más pequeño.

**Próximo paso** – El Fondo de Financiamiento de Observaciones Sistemáticas (SOFF) de la ONU está trabajando para financiar y apoyar estaciones meteorológicas en estos países, con el objetivo de cerrar las brechas en la red global y mejorar la seguridad y las predicciones en todo el mundo.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Apoyar la recopilación de datos meteorológicos en países pobres fortalece las predicciones globales, haciendo que las predicciones sean más precisas para todos.

articles.title: Press release - COP31: MEPs urge all parties to implement climate change commitments
articles.summary: Before leaving the UN Climate Change Conference in Antalya, the MEPs leading Parliament’s delegation commented on the status of the negotiations.Committee on the Environment, Public Health and Food SafetyCommittee on Industry, Research and Energy Source : © European Union, 2026 - EP
articles.content:
An official delegation from the European Parliament has been in Antalya, Türkiye this week at the UN Climate Change Conference, COP31.

Delegation Chair Lídia Pereira (EPP, PT) and vice-chair Heléne Fritzon (S&D, SE) made the following comments ahead of the final stretch of negotiations.

“COP31 must be the COP of implementation. Our meetings this week with countries from across the world, from major economies to the most vulnerable island states, confirmed that Europe has strong partners for this agenda. But while the draft cover decision points in the right direction on electrification, we cannot accept a text that no longer even refers to what we all agreed at COP28 on transitioning away from fossil fuels. As negotiations enter their final hours, Europe must keep pushing, because decarbonisation is not only a climate necessity, it is our best driver of growth and energy security,” said Lídia Pereira (EPP, PT), delegation chair.

“As Parliament’s delegation, we have had two jobs: to push the Commission in fighting all the way for higher ambition, and to raise our priorities with other countries. We have had many interesting exchanges – and some tough discussions – with Brazil, China, South Africa and the incoming Ethiopian COP32 presidency, as well as with civil society, including on new climate targets and carbon pricing systems emerging elsewhere. The COPs remain our most important tool for climate multilateralism, and we are moving forward. But the pace is too slow. As warming is set to overshoot 1.5°C, we must really deliver on our promises,” said Heléne Fritzon (S&D, SE), delegation vice-chair.

A press conference with delegation chair Lídia Pereira and EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra took place on Wednesday 18 November. You can watch a recording here.

On Thursday 19 November, the European Parliament hosted a side event at the EU Pavilion on “Electrification for energy security and for economic and climate resilience”. You can watch a recording of it here.

Background

COP31 is taking place in Antalya from 9 to 20 November 2026. Türkiye holds the COP31 presidency, with Minister of Environment, Urbanisation and Climate Change Murat Kurum as President, while Australia’s Minister for Climate Change and Energy, Chris Bowen, is President of Negotiations.

In February 2026, Parliament approved an amendment to the European Climate Law setting a legally binding target of reducing net greenhouse gas emissions by 90% by 2040 compared to 1990 levels, with at least 85% to be achieved within the EU. The law entered into force in April 2026.

Parliament is a co-legislator on EU energy and climate legislation, which seeks to implement the Paris Agreement, and before the EU can enter international agreements Parliament must give its consent.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on the European Parliament delegation's active role at COP31, urging implementation of climate commitments and stronger ambition on decarbonization. It highlights meaningful international cooperation and legally binding EU climate targets, indicating significant real-world impact on climate action with broad societal benefits.
articles.personality_title: European Parliament pushes for stronger climate action at COP31
articles.personality_presentation:

**What happened** – The European Parliament’s delegation, led by Lídia Pereira and Heléne Fritzon, spoke out during the conference. They stressed the need to turn promises into real actions, especially moving away from fossil fuels and increasing the use of clean electricity. They also met with leaders from countries like Brazil, China, and South Africa to discuss new climate goals and ways to reduce carbon emissions. The Parliament hosted events to promote energy security through electrification.

**Impact** – This is important because the European Parliament has set a strong law to cut greenhouse gas emissions by 90% by 2040, which is one of the toughest targets worldwide. Their active role at COP31 shows Europe’s commitment to leading global climate efforts and encouraging other countries to do the same. The focus on electrification and decarbonization supports both the environment and economic growth, helping protect energy supplies.

After COP31, attention will turn to how these decisions get put into practice, especially within the EU, where laws will guide the changes.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The European Parliament is actively urging global leaders at COP31 to turn climate promises into strong actions, focusing on clean energy and deep emission cuts by 2040.

articles.personality_title_es: El Parlamento Europeo impulsa una acción climática más fuerte en la COP31
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La Conferencia de las Naciones Unidas sobre el Cambio Climático, llamada COP31, se celebra en Antalya, Turquía, del 9 al 20 de noviembre de 2026. Países de todo el mundo se reúnen para hablar sobre cómo enfrentar el cambio climático. El Parlamento Europeo envió un equipo para compartir los planes de Europa.

El Parlamento organizó eventos para promover la seguridad energética mediante la electrificación.

**Impacto** – Esto es importante porque el Parlamento Europeo ha establecido una ley fuerte para reducir las emisiones de gases de efecto invernadero en un 90 % para 2040, uno de los objetivos más estrictos del mundo. Su papel activo en la COP31 muestra el compromiso de Europa para liderar los esfuerzos climáticos globales y animar a otros países a hacer lo mismo. El enfoque en la electrificación y la descarbonización apoya tanto al medio ambiente como al crecimiento económico, ayudando a proteger el suministro de energía.

**Próximo paso** – Las negociaciones en la COP31 están entrando en su fase final, donde los países decidirán las acciones exactas que tomarán.
